A typical battery that is the same size as a gallon of gas (0.134 cubic feet) can store only 15.3% of the gallon of gas’s energy when used for transportation (AFDC 2024). This will require more frequent vehicle downtime for charging (as compared to previous refueling intervals) and changes to transportation plans to account for the added weight of the energy systems needed by forward-deployed units. Investing in research and development to improve power density would mitigate this risk over the longer term. 3.6 Nascent Infrastructure and Capacity Like any new technology, advanced energy infrastructure and manufacturing capacity are expanding along with adoption. Infrastructure and supply development for some advanced energy technologies is still inadequate for forecasted demand, creating insufficient infrastructure, escalating costs, and increasing supply chain disruption risks for the large-scale DOW commitment to these technologies. Examples include the following: • Hydrogen fuel is not yet widely adopted in the commercial sector, so finding refueling or maintenance parts during deployment would be challenging. The small U.S. hydrogen market and underdeveloped customer support may dampen adoption despite hydrogen’s technical promise. • Although there is significant overcapacity in Li-ion battery cell manufacturing at the global scale, U.S. capacity is still emerging. According to projections by Argonne National Laboratory, U.S. Li-ion battery cell manufacturing capacity will reach 210 gigawatt hours (GWh) in 2025, supplying roughly 30–50% of North American demand. Domestic manufacturing capacity for battery cell components (e.g., anodes, cathodes, electrolyte, foils, and separators) is even more nascent, with insufficient planned North American component production to fully supply announced battery cell production (Gohlke et al. 2024). DOW could face escalating costs and supply chain disruptions, impacting the mission. • The domestic production capacity of synthetic aviation fuel (SAF) (also known as sustainable aviation fuel) does not currently meet domestic demand (Rosales Calderon et al. 2024a, 2024b) or potential military demand. Although the domestic SAF supply chain is growing, unclear capacity growth contributes to market uncertainty (Rosales Calderon et al. 2024a, 2024b). DOW could face fuel shortages if SAF becomes a requirement. For more details on SAF, see Appendix G. 3.7 Evolving Standards Gaps in standards are inherent risks in any major technological transition, and the shift to advanced energy systems is no exception, creating potential safety, security, and cost risks for DOW. If they are not addressed, these gaps could lead to incidents (e.g., fires or cyber intrusions) that degrade mission readiness and have even more severe consequences during conflict. Moreover, unless military logistics considerations are integrated into standards early on, manufacturers might produce advanced energy technologies that are unrealistic for use during deployments, limiting resilience and energy security benefits. 10 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Without timely, consistent standards, advanced technologies like hydrogen fuel systems and interconnected energy networks such as microgrids could introduce vulnerabilities before appropriate safeguards are in place.
